chunks: He is the One who destroys it after its existence,
until that which exists in it becomes like that which is lost.
And the perishing of the world after its creation is no more wondrous than its formation and invention,

even if all the animals of it, from its birds and beasts, and what is of its stabled and pasturing [animals], and the kinds, origins, and species of it, and its dull and sagacious peoples, were to gather to create a mosquito, they would not be able to create it,
nor would they know the way to its creation,
and their intellects would be bewildered in knowing that and wander, and their powers would become weak and fail,
and they would return disgraced and regretful, knowing that they are conquered, admitting their inability to create it, and submitting to their weakness in destroying it!
ai.seo_question: How can the destruction of the world be considered strange when its creation is so complex?
ai.summary: Sharif al-Radi presents this passage as a logical proof of divine omnipotence, contrasting the collective inability of all living beings to create a single mosquito with God's effortless power to annihilate the entire cosmos. This argument underscores the concept of *Qudra* (Power) by highlighting human intellectual bewilderment and submission to the Creator's absolute sovereignty over existence and non-existence.

en.sayed-ali-raza: He will destroy the earth after its existence, till all that exists on it will become non-existent.
But the extinction of the world after its creation is no stranger than its first formation and invention.

Even if all the animals of the earth, whether birds or beasts, stabled cattle or pasturing ones, of different origins and species, dull people and sagacious men — all jointly try to create (even) a mosquito they are not able to bring it into being and do not understand what is the way to its creation.

Their wits are bewildered and wandering. Their powers fall short and fail, and return disappointed and tired, knowing that they are defeated and admitting their inability to produce it, also realizing that they are too weak (even) to destroy it.
